paragraphs: Since economy is connected with the subject of revenue, it is fitting to consider it next. Money saved on one object can be put to good use on another, and so much less will need to be taken from the pockets of the people. If the States are united under one government, there will be only one national civil list to support (the cost of maintaining the civil government). If they are divided into several confederacies, there will be as many separate national civil lists to provide for, and each of them, in its principal departments, will be as large as the one a government of the whole would need. The complete separation of the States into thirteen unconnected sovereignties is too extravagant a project, and too full of danger, to have many advocates. Men who speculate about the breakup of the empire generally seem to have in mind three confederacies: one made up of the four Northern States, another of the four Middle States, and a third of the five Southern States. There is little likelihood that there would be more than that. On this division, each confederacy would cover a territory larger than the kingdom of Great Britain. No well-informed man will suppose that the affairs of such a confederacy could be properly managed by a government less comprehensive in its organs and institutions than the one proposed by the Convention. When a State reaches a certain size, it needs the same energy of government and the same forms of administration that are required in a much larger one. This idea cannot be demonstrated precisely, because there is no rule by which we can measure the force of civil power needed to govern any given number of people. But consider that the island of Britain, nearly equal in size to each of the supposed confederacies, contains about eight millions of people. Consider also the degree of authority required to direct the passions of so large a society toward the public good. We shall then see no reason to doubt that the same amount of power would be enough to do the same task in a society far more numerous. Civil power, properly organized and exercised, can spread its force over a very great extent. By a judicious arrangement of subordinate institutions, it can in a manner reproduce itself in every part of a great empire.

The supposition that each confederacy into which the States would likely be divided would need a government as comprehensive as the one proposed is strengthened by another supposition, more probable than the one that offers us three confederacies as the alternative to a general Union. If we pay careful attention to geographical and commercial considerations, together with the habits and prejudices of the different States, we shall conclude that in case of disunion they would most naturally join themselves under two governments. The four Eastern States, for all the reasons that form the links of national sympathy and connection, can be expected with certainty to unite. New York, situated as she is, would never be so unwise as to present a feeble and unsupported flank to the weight of that confederacy. There are other obvious reasons that would make it easier for her to join it. New Jersey is too small a State to think of being a frontier against this still more powerful combination, and there seem to be no obstacles to her admission into it. Even Pennsylvania would have strong inducements to join the Northern league. An active foreign commerce, based on her own shipping, is her true policy, and it agrees with the opinions and dispositions of her citizens. The more Southern States, for various reasons, may not consider themselves much interested in encouraging shipping. They may prefer a system that would give all nations unlimited freedom to be the carriers as well as the purchasers of their commodities. Pennsylvania may not choose to merge her interests in a connection so opposed to her policy. Since she must in any case be a frontier, she may judge it most consistent with her safety to turn her exposed side toward the weaker power of the Southern Confederacy rather than toward the stronger power of the Northern. This would give her the best chance to avoid being the Flanders of America. Whatever Pennsylvania decides, if the Northern Confederacy includes New Jersey, there is no likelihood of more than one confederacy to the south of that State.

Nothing can be more evident than that the thirteen States will be able to support a national government better than one half of them, or one third, or any number less than the whole. This reflection must carry great weight against the objection to the proposed plan that rests on the principle of expense. When we look at that objection more closely, however, it will appear in every light to stand on mistaken ground.

Consider, in addition to the plurality of civil lists, the number of persons who would necessarily be employed to guard the inland communication between the different confederacies against illicit trade. In time they will inevitably arise out of the needs of revenue. Consider also the military establishments which, as has been shown, would unavoidably result from the jealousies and conflicts of the separate nations into which the States would be divided. We shall then clearly see that a separation would be no less injurious to the economy than to the tranquillity, commerce, revenue, and liberty of every part.
